Press Release:


“Rhodes must fall”
Calls for the removal of a Cecil John Rhodes statue at UCT have escalated into hefty debate over transformation and, subsequently, allegations of lack of transformation in universities. To some, it’s a symbol of an oppressive white colonial past. To others it’s much ado about nothing. But has this all sparked a long overdue self-examination exercise into race, heritage and identity? Carte Blanche investigates.
Watch the clip.


Script:


He had being planning his action for a year. Fed up by what he believes is a lack of transformation at the University of Cape Town, and disturbed by recent racists attacks in the city. Chumani Maxwele the 9th of March threw feces at the statue of a Cecil john Rhodes as a form of ultimate protest,

Chumani Maxwele: It’s a question of historical black pain, black humiliation and of course the institutional racism at uct. Very direct.

Hundreds of protesting students have demanded that statue, which was covered in plastic for most of last week, be torn down. Its provoked rowdy debate between students who have different views on the statues future. The most vocal are those who want to see it toppled.

For example in Germany you don’t see statues of Hitler around
I believe the statue should come down
The response of the administration has been pathetic
The statue must come down

It’s also resulted on appalling racist posts and tweets on social media.
On Wednesday 20th March angry students marched to the administration center of the university demanding the removal of the statue. They were also are calling for different curiculum and a more black lecturers.

Link: The bremner building has become the focal point of the student protest here at uct with as many as 100 staging a sleep in. They say that they won’t leave until their demands are met. The university has decided not to take any action against them so as to avoid a possible escalation.


The vice chancellor has had hands full this week.
John: Dr. price it’s been a difficult few days for you. How are you feeling?
Max Price. It’s tiring, bit stressed but also quite invigorating. It’s a level of activism that i've always hoped we would see in students. The worst thing to have is apathetic students.

Chumani Maxwele is certainly not an apathetic student when it comes to Cecil john Rhodes.

Chumani Maxwele: HE will just tell you that he doesn’t want black people. He exploited them. He brutally killed them. He brutally dispossessed black people and then for him it was clear. Now we have very subtle racism, which is not different from Cecil John Rhodes racism.

LINK: This statue occupies pride of place here at UCT but not in the minds of many of the students that go tot his university. So what is it about this man and his legacy that ahs so many people up in arms?

British born Cecil john Rhode was a towering and controversial figure who dominated commerce and politics in the Western Cape in the late 1800s, ending up as Prime Minister of the Cape Colony. In response to the student stand off at UCT, the Centre for conflict resolution invited professor Paul Maylam, who has written a book on the imperialist to address an audience at a public debate in Cape Town earlier this week.

Paul Maylam: He was the arch imperialist who rode rough shored over indigenous African peoples. He was the mining magnate who saw African workers as no more than units of labor and he was a politician, he was prime minister of the cape in the 1890's. Some people say he was a forerunner of segregation and apartheid.


For example he said: the native is to be treated as a child and denied the franchise. We must adopt a system of despotism in our relations with the barbarians of South Africa. He also used offensive language to describe black people.


There is a history though of other groups wanting the statue removed.

Max Price: Afrikaans students in the 30's 40's 50's and still today think that Rhodes was an awful person who waged war against the Boer republics and white radical students used to pain the statue, call for its removal in the 70's and 80's. What's changed is that we have a critical mass of people who feel so strongly about it.

One of the studentd prtesotors occupying Bremner building is Mbali Matandela. She’s offended by the statue and points out that it is positioned to gaze over the cape flat, historically one of the poorest and most marginilised areas of Cape Town.

Mbali Matandela: And I cant walk past there without feeling all the different layers from the different generations that have been oppressed by some form of colonization and when I walk past there I feel those different levels of pain and it comes out as rage.


She is also angry about what she perceives as the racist attitude of some students towards black professors.

Mbali: When this one Ghanaian black professor was in the front of the class presenting his lecture, you hear students laughing at him on the side because they are like we don’t understand him so clearly his knowledge is not credible.

Debate has been ignited. Radio talk shows have been dominated by the subject. Many have voiced their disgust at the use of feces as a form of protest.

Chumani: The human feces for us is a metaphoric thing. We are bringing our pain.

Chumani Maxwele says that the throwing of human feces is the ultimate expression of the humiliation and pain felt by many poor capetoninans who are forced to use porta loos. A legacy of apartheid and a sign he says that racism still exists.

Long serving uct lecturer Dr Tzili Reisenberger who was caught up the in protest empathizes with the students but she says she doesn’t always agree with their methods.

Tzili: The best way for a debate is suggest how to come forward. Not by destroying something but saying I also want something like this, maybe we'll work it together. Maybe ill also have a voice or something. That is my hope.

Link: To borrow a phrase the best thing about the internet is that everyone can have a say and the worst thing about the internet is that everybody can have a say and no better was that demonstrated than in the vitriol that appeared on social media around the rhodesmustfall campaign.

Many of the tweets were offensive and represented hate speech. Some of them which were tweeted from the campus were read out.

Sounds Up

The racist tweets proved too much for Mbali.

Mbali: I just can’t believe that I’ve been sitting in the same room of people who think of things like this about me. Who think that I am less of a person. I just feel so dehumanised and I feel like an object and less of a student.

Max Price: But what I have been hearing which I think is important to correct is comments especially on talk in radio is that these students are lucky to be at uct, that they should be studying. That they are actual going to fail or that they got in on 30% pass marks from school.

In fact the students staging a sleep in are using some of the time to keep up with their studies. They are also visited by academics who hold discussion forums about the issues affecting the university and country.

Max Price: These are intelligent serious articulate well thought out students. They are students who I find inspiring.

Equally inspired is uct sociology professor Xolele Mangcu who supports the students cause. He says that this protest is about far more than just a statue.

Xolele Mangcu: Our students are complaining. They are complaining of racial abuse. They are complaining of attitudes on the part of professors on the one hand. But they are also complaining of not having people they can relate to whose background they can relate to, who can understand their languages.

He is one of only 5 black South African professors at the institution. According to last year’s figures, there were 148 white prof4ssors at uct.

Max Price: The staff demography is almost unchanged for the last 5-10 years and that is not a uct problem, it is a national problem. I've talked before about the fact that there are only 34 South African born black women professors in the whole country. We have programs in place to accelerate those career paths but I think we can do more.

Professor Mangcu says these figures should make it clear to the university that debate on what the stature represents and its future is unnecessary.
He says that the stature should come down and come down now.

Xolele Mangcu: A university should stake out a very clear moral position like universities have done throughout history.

Dr Price agrees that the statue must be moved but that a process needs to be followed first.

MaxPrice: To take a view that there is nothing to discuss and that a vocal articulate group should simply have their way is antithetical to everything a university is.

Link: Cecil John Rhodes was a man of contradictions and complicating the debate is the fact that according to his supporters, he also had a generous side. Rhodes bequeathed vast tracks of land to the people of South Africa and even the university of Cape Town is on land he donated. Thanks to the Rhodes scholarship, thousands of students around the world have graduated from Oxford University. A more recent collaboration, the Mandela Rhodes scholarship is helping African scholars like Siphisile Dumisa to complete their studies in this country.

Siphisile: We recognize Rhodes’s entrepreneurial spirit and we also appreciate the value that he places on education. Although Rhodes never intended for someone like me be a beneficiary of his trust. But today I am. Whatever he thinks is either here nor there but the fact of the matter is that that money is being used to contribute towards the education of students and citizens who will contribute positively to our country.


Professor Maylam agrees that Rhodes may have had more selfish motives

Paul Maylam: And I think he probably saw scholarships as a means to achieve that immortality and they have succeeded. And if the statues go, the memorials go, the scholarships won’t.

What started as a one-man protest at the university of Cape Town has reverberated around the country? Similar protests against colonial names and statues have taken place at other universities. Then on Friday the university senate overwhelmingly voted for the removal of the statue. But professor Mangcu says that the events on campus should be a wake up call for all South Africans.

Xolele Mangcu: its quite frightening for as along as the voices of black people are not taken seriously and that is what is beginning to happen now and I fear for this country. I fear that people too often take for granted the peace that we have.
